author: Anand
asr_identification: candidates Juafardih, Jagdishpur, Saure, Rukmanisthan (Nalanda district, Bihar); Juafardih 'most promising'
evidence: On the ground: mounds at all four villages; NBPW sherds in quantity on the surface at Juafardih and Jagdishpur, nothing earlier than Pāla at Saure and Rukmanisthan; photographs of the Jagdishpur mound and of the 2007 Juafardih dig. Reported (ASI 2007 excavation, Saran): a mud stūpa of the Buddha's period at the core of the Juafardih mound, enlarged in mud and capped by a Kuṣāṇa–Śuṅga brick stūpa, no relic casket. Argument: distances plotted from Nālandā (8–9 li SW) and back from Naṇand/Chaṇdimau (taken as Śāriputra's village).
quote: All the four villages have mounds and as far as Potshards are concerned Juafardih and Jagdishpur has NBPW in large quantities. Saure and Rukmanisthan don’t have any potshards earlier than Pala period on surface. Juafardih one of the most promising sites was excavated in 2007 and it had a mud stupa at the heart which belonged to Buddha period.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs from the study (unidentified; Cunningham's Jagdispur mound unconfirmed) only by adding Juafardih, whose excavation the study does not yet use (primary: Saran, Purātattva 38, 2008; IAR 2006–07). Text slip: writes 8–9 li 'NW' then 'SW' (Xuanzang: SW). Mizutani: no site.

author: Anand
asr_identification: Juafardīh (25°08′06″ N, 85°25′54″ E) = the excavated stūpa; unexcavated 1-acre mound W of Jagdishpur (25°07′36″ N, 85°25′18″ E), 1 km SW, = the second (relic) stūpa; Nalanda district
evidence: Reported, not his own: ASI excavation 2007 of the 10-m-high, 105 × 100 m mound at Juafardīh: a stūpa from the 5th c. BCE with later rebuildings; a broken disc with two Brāhmī letters read 'MUGA' (Saran 2008, Purātattva 38: 59–73); no relics. Own argument: since no relics were found, the second stūpa with Maudgalyāyana's relics should be the Jagdishpur mound; aerial photographs of both (Guichard 2007).
quote: the Archaeological Survey of India excavated the 10mt high mound measuring 105mt x 100mt located at Juafardīh (25° 08' 06'' N. 85° 25' 54'' E). The excavation revealed the mound to be a stūpa site from the time of the Buddha (5th BCE) with successive reconstructions in later periods. Among the rich antiquities unearthed during excavation was a broken disc bearing two brāhmī letters ‘MUGA’
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs: the study leaves Kolika unidentified (Cunningham's Jagdispur mound unconfirmed); Anand follows Saran's Juafardih and keeps Jagdishpur for the relic stūpa. The 'MUGA' disc is the only inscriptional pointer offered; check Saran 2008 and IAR 2006–07 for the reading and context. Mizutani: no site.

author: Anand
name_in_asr: ‘meeting place’ (Bimbisāra welcomes the Buddha), 3–4 li E of Kūlika
asr_identification: village Kūl (25°06′49″ N, 85°27′32″ E), c. 4 km SE of Jagdishpur, c. 2.5 km S of Nālandā
evidence: On the ground: an ancient mound and an ancient Buddha image at Kūl (photographs Guichard 2005). Argument: Pāli sources put the Buddha–Mahākassapa meeting (Bahuputtaka Nigrodha) between Rājagaha and Nālandā, three gāvutas from Veḷuvana; Silāo, where a Pāla image inscribed with the 'exchange of robes' was found (Chhabra, EI 25: 327–333), lies halfway; he holds that Xuanzang's Bimbisāra stūpa was originally the Mahākassapa meeting place. Admits Kūl fits neither the Record's distance and bearing nor the Life's.
quote: The first potential archaeological site eastward of Jagdishpur that may represent the ‘meeting place’ is village Kūl (25° 06' 49'' N. 85° 27' 32'' E) … It is evident, that Kūl does not match the distance and direction descriptions of the ‘meeting place’ mentioned in the biography (Beal 1914) or the travelogues (Rongxi 1996) of Xuanzang.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. New place: the stūpa where Bimbisāra met the Buddha (頻毘娑羅王迎佛處), between 09.03.08 and 09.03.10, not in places.tsv. Anand's own test fails on distance and bearing; a candidate only.

author: Anand
asr_identification: Naṇand (25°05′27″ N, 85°30′11″ E), Nalanda district (after Prasad 1988), rather than Chaṇdimau 3 km S (Broadley)
evidence: On the ground: Naṇand is a large village on ancient remains, with ancient images and a votive stūpa but no surviving prominent mound; Chaṇdimau has an excavated mound and images (some in the Indian Museum, Kolkata). Deciding test: a mound 1–2 km SE for the disciples' stūpa exists near Naṇand (Shobhāpur, row 4) but none within 1–2 km SE of Chaṇdimau. Both lie c. 15 km W of Pārbati, which he takes as Indraśailaguhā (Chaudhari 1936).
quote: It is generally accepted that either of the villages Naṇand (Prasad 1988:175) or Chaṇdimau (Broadley 1979: 51) may represent the village of Sāriputta mentioned by Faxian and Xuanzang … According to my observations, village Naṇand is most likely the village of Sāriputta.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs: the study has no site for 09.03.10 (Mizutani none; Ji: Sarichak). Primary: Prasad, East and West 38 (1988): 175–188; Broadley, Buddhistic Remains of Bihar. The choice rests on the Shobhāpur mound and on Pārbati as Indraśailaguhā, which the study does not accept (09.03.11 = Giriyek).

author: Anand
name_in_asr: place where Śāriputra's disciples entered nirvāṇa, 4–5 li SE of Kālapināka
asr_identification: large mound NW of Shobhāpur (25°05′12″ N, 85°31′15″ E), E bank of the Panchāne, 1.8 km E of Naṇand
evidence: On the ground: a 'huge mound' with potsherds at Shobhāpur, found by his own exploration of villages 1–2.5 km S, E and SE of Naṇand and Chaṇdimau; no comparable mound SE of Chaṇdimau. Not excavated.
quote: I found a huge mound in village Shobhāpur (25° 05' 12'' N. 85° 31' 15'' E) situated 1.8km as the crow flies east of Naṇand. The mound is situated a little northwest of Shobhāpur on the eastern bank of river Panchane. I didn't find any potential mound within the specified distance of 1-2 km SE of Chaṇdimau.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. New place: the stūpa of Śāriputra's disciples' nirvāṇa (SE of 迦羅臂拏迦邑), not in places.tsv. The mound lies E, not SE, of Naṇand by his own coordinates.

author: Anand
asr_identification: isolated hill of Pārbati (25°05′06″ N, 85°39′05″ E), after P. C. Chaudhari 1936
evidence: No field evidence given here; cites Chaudhari, JBORS 22 (1936): 302, and Faxian's yojana from Nāla.
quote: The isolated hill of village Pārbati (25° 05' 06'' N. 85° 39' 05'' E) has been identified as the site of Indraśailaguhā (Chaudhari 1936: 302).
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs: the study keeps Giriyek for 09.03.11 (goose figures, Haṃsa stūpa, Gidhadwar cave) and puts Kapotaka (09.03.13) at Parbati. Chaudhari 1936 is not yet in the study.

author: Anand
asr_identification: Barui (25°09′12″ N, 85°54′39″ E), at the N foot of Pachnā hill, E end of the Sheikhpurā range, Sheikhpura district, Bihar
evidence: On the ground (visit 6 May 2024): at Barui a mosque and graveyard on a brick mound c. 12 ft high over a quarter acre, bricks looking ancient (not measured), 'like the remains of a stūpa'; the village centre on raised ground; a broken Buddha at the Middle School and image fragments at Mahārāni Sthān. At Pachnā village (S of the hill): an inscribed Vajratārā (11th–12th c.; Tribedy, Journal of Bengal Art 26, 2021) dug up in May 2020 and probably planted at its findspot; a crowned Buddha inscribed 8th–9th c. and a life-size Buddha head from the 25-acre Pokhara (2022); Directorate of Archaeology, Bihar, site inspection report 2020. Kāre-Matokhar hill (explored 2011): Brahmanical only. Distance: Barui c. 45 km from Nālandā (= 150–160 li), only 27 km from Pārbati, so he takes the Life's route from Nālandā over the Record's from Indraśailaguhā.
quote: Pachnā-Barui is the only known village in the Seikhpurā range of hills that has ancient Buddhist images in view and a potential stūpa mound in Barui … Barui is almost 45 km as the crow flies from the ancient remains of Nālandā, equivalent to 150-160 Li confirming the descriptions of Xuanzang.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs: the study puts Kapotaka at Parbati (Cunningham ASR XV: pigeon name, bearing, saṅgha seal); Mizutani at Bihār. Anand's case needs Pārbati = Indraśailaguhā and measures the distance from Nālandā, not from the hill; he calls it his 'best-educated guess', finds 'not very encouraging' and no monastic remains yet.

author: Anand
name_in_asr: isolated hill S of Kapotaka (Avalokiteśvara temple)
asr_identification: Pachnā hill (25°09′ N, 85°54′ E), E end of the Sheikhpurā range, now largely quarried away
evidence: On the ground: the hill mined since c. 2014, the part with a 'cave-like structure' and a flat top with brickbats (seen by Directorate staff in 2020; Tribedy 2021: 716) lost to mining in 2023; late-medieval sherds reported on the hill; villagers recall the hill as tall and steep. No remains of shrines at the Vajratārā findspot.
quote: The large-scale mining of Pachnā Hill is a recent phenomenon that started around a decade ago. The people recall a cave-like structure atop the hill that contained ancient remains … This part of the Hill with the ‘cave’ and flat surface with brickbats was lost to mining in 2023.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs: the study's hill is the Parbati hill, site A (dargah of Haji Chandar). Follows from row 1; the hill's remains can no longer be tested.

author: Anand
asr_identification: Pārbati hill (after Chaudhari 1936), not Cunningham's Giriyak
evidence: No field evidence; reports Chaudhari, JBORS 22 (1936): 302 as 'now accepted'.
quote: More than a half-century later P C Choudhary proposed that Pārbati Hill may be the Indraśailaguhā and not Kapotaka as proposed by Cunningham (Chaudhari 1936: 302). Pārbati Hill is now accepted as the correct identification of Indraśailaguhā.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs from the study (Giriyek; Parbati = Kapotaka). 'Now accepted' is asserted without citing who accepts it.

author: Anand
name_in_asr: big village south of the Gaṅgā
asr_identification: Rajaonā–Chouki–Valgūdar (Rajaonā 25°11′ N, 86°05′ E), 3 km NE of Lakhisarai station, Lakhisarai district = ancient Kṛmilā/Kimbilā
evidence: On the ground (visit 31 July 2024): the Rajaonā–Chouki mound estimated at c. 200 acres (survey and Google Earth); c. 60 old tanks reported; Brahmanical and Buddhist sculptures in village sheds; well-bores NE of the village and brick kilns E of Valgūdar reported to reach white Ganges sand at c. 12 ft, the mound's steep N face read as an old concave river bank. Cited: Cunningham's Chouki mound pillars (ASR III: 153–154; Asher 1986: Gupta); Kṛmilā inscriptions from Valgūdar and Rajaonā (Sircar, EI 28: 137–145; Sircar 1971: 248–255); 22+ mounds within 5 km (Anil Kumar; Kumar 2011, IHR 38); NBPW (Chattopadhyay & Sanyal 2008); 7th–13th-c. sculptures (Bandyopadhyay, Chattopadhyay & Majumder 2015). Distance: 13–20 km from his candidate Hīnayāna monastery, 18 km NE of Barui.
quote: In my opinion, Rajaonā ​​(25° 11' N. 86° 05' E) which is 13-20 km from the potential location of the Hinayāna Monastery (i.e., the group of villages Imādnagar, Bakiyābād etc.) and 18 km northeast of Barui, as the crow flies, is most likely the site of the prosperous village by the Gaṅgā.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs: the study has Shekhpura for 09.03.15a (Cunningham ASR XV; low) and Rajaona for Lāvaṇīla (09.03.15b). Anand's chain starts from Barui = Kapotaka and Pārbati = Indraśailaguhā. The Ganges-sand reports are hearsay from farmers, not a section he saw; Kṛmilā is an inscribed place-name, but not a Xiyu ji name.

author: Anand
name_in_asr: great stūpa SE of the big village
asr_identification: mound beside the Banyāhi Pokhara (25°11′34″ N, 86°04′52″ E), SE edge of the Rajaonā–Chouki mound
evidence: On the ground: a projecting mound (two mounds levelled into one for cultivation) being ploughed, brickbats all around, a small inscribed broken Buddha under a tree and another Buddha in a shrine, both said by the Mānjhi community to come from the mound. He takes it for one of the two mounds E of Rajaonā where Cunningham (ASR XV: 14) saw a Buddha and a Padmapāṇi; rejects the Brindāban stūpa mound (4 km SE) as too far.
quote: I trust the mound adjacent to Banyāhi Pokhara is the stūpa mound noted by Cunningham, and most likely the remains of the great stūpa mentioned by Xuanzang … However, sans archaeological excavations, these are just an informed supposition.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. New place: the great stūpa near the big village (大聚落東南不遠), not in places.tsv. In the study these are Cunningham's northern mounds at Rajaona that support Lāvaṇīla (09.03.15b), not 09.03.15a.

author: Anand
name_in_asr: Hinayāna monastery (40 li SE of Kapotaka)
asr_identification: unsurveyed candidates 8–13 km SE of Barui: Mahsaurā, Nadiyāwān, Bhamariyā, Bartārā, Imādnagar, Bakiyābād, Asthāwan, Benguchhā
evidence: None; a list of villages within range, survey deferred.
quote: Eight to thirteen kilometres southeast of Barui leads us to several potential villages like Mahsaurā, Nadiyāwān, Bhamariyā, Bartārā, Imādnagar, Bakiyābād, Asthāwan and Benguchhā etc., that could represent the site of Hinayāna monastery mentioned by Xuanzang
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs in base point only (the study: Aphsar if Kapotaka = Parbati, Tetrawa if Bihār); no site proposed.

author: Anand
asr_identification: rejects Giriyak (Indraśailaguhā) and Rajaonā (Lāvaṇīla); the chain is moved E from Pārbati
evidence: Argument only: Giriyak is the W end of the Rājgir range, not an isolated hill, and lies S, not E, of Nālandā; once Pārbati is Indraśailaguhā, Cunningham's later sites (Matokhar Tāl as the big village, Rajaonā as Lāvaṇīla) all shift E.
quote: Giriyak Hill is neither an isolated hill nor situated east of Nālandā … The identification of Pārbati Hill as Indraśailaguhā invalidates the identification of all the subsequent sites following Indraśailaguhā like Matakhar Tāl (Village by the Gaṅgā) and Rajaonā (Lāvaṇīla) offered by Cunningham
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs: the study keeps Giriyek for 09.03.11 and Rajaona for 09.03.15b. His summary of Cunningham is partly wrong: he says Cunningham first took Tetrāwan as Kapotaka (Cunningham 1871 gave Bihār; Titarawa was the Hīnayāna monastery, 09.03.15). The objection that Giriyak is S of Nālandā deserves a check against Xuanzang's route (30 li E from the disciples' stūpa).

author: Anand
asr_identification: Indapegaḍh (Indape fort, 24°53′ N, 86°13′ E), W of the Kiul near its junction with the Barnar, Lakhisarai/Jamui, Bihar; Nōṇgaḍh equally possible
evidence: On the ground (visit Aug 2024): at Indape a stūpa mound (Buchanan's 'temple of a Buoddh'; Beglar: 125 ft across, 35 ft high) and the 'lofty terrace' (220 × 110 ft) both cut into for school buildings; large bricks reused in houses; a Buddha in a village collective; a villager says the Buddha images now in Jamui Museum came from the terrace. Cited: four terracotta Padmapāṇi medallions from the stūpa given to the Indian Museum in 1882 (Anderson 1883: 95); 7th-c. Buddha images, the only ones of that date in the Lakhisarai region (Asher 1988; Bautze-Picron 1991–92: 239, 242); BRW, NBPW, BPW around the fort (Chattopadhyay & Sanyal 2008: 264–265). Distances: Indape 36 km SE of Rajaonā (= 100+ li) with hills between, 60 km SW of Munger. No lake of 30 li circuit exists N of either site, so he suspects Xuanzang did not go to Lāvaṇīla.
quote: Nōṇgaḍh and Indapegaḍh are ancient Buddhist sites and equally probable to be the ancient Lāvaṇīla, yet, I trust the ancient remains of Indapegaḍh represent the Buddhist remains of Lāvaṇīla … Nōṇgaḍh is 17 km and Indapegaḍh is 36 km as the crow flies southeast of Rajaonā
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs: the study has Rajjana/Rajaona (Cunningham ASR XV; medium), whose case rests on the lake to the N, the Buddhist remains and the onward distance to Monghyr; Anand moves the start to Rajaonā as the big village (09.03.15a) and reads 'east' as SE. Note the bibliography summary (biblio_D) says he argues for Nongarh; the post prefers Indapegaḍh.

author: Anand
asr_identification: Nōṇgaḍh (25°03′ N, 86°08′ E), W bank of the Kiul, Lakhisarai district: 'stūpa mound' (Mā Bhagwati Sthān) and 'monastery mound'
evidence: On the ground (6 Aug 2024): the 'stūpa mound' now under 30 ft; villagers say six yakṣī images came out of it (three in 1961, three in 1995 from two brick-robbing trenches on its SW slope, found upright on a plaster floor), now in the Bābā Mitrasen Sthān, Jamui Museum or stolen (1998); yakṣa images from the river said to come from the eroded 'monastery mound'; Buddhist images (two Avalokiteśvaras, a seated Buddha, Jamui Museum) said to come from the mound under the Maṭh, 400 m S. Cited: Cunningham ASR III: 161 (40-ft mound, two chambers with eleven unburnt clay stūpas); Beglar ASR VIII: 119 (an early N-facing temple inside); Asher 2000 (Artibus Asiae 59) for Nongarh as Lāvaṇīla; Chattopadhyay & Bandyopadhyay 2017 (no stūpa plan; BRW to EMRW); a 12th-c. pedestal inscription naming the place Ḍakā (Sircar 1970: 41–42). He concludes the 'stūpa' was a yakṣī shrine later encased as a stūpa.
quote: The question is, does Nōṇgaḍh represent Lāvaṇīla as proposed by Cunningham? Well, Fredrick Asher believes so (Asher 2000: 302) … It is important to note that this inscription from the 12th CE refers to this locality of Nōṇgaḍh as Ḍakā and not Lāvaṇīla.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Bears against Nongarh, one of Cunningham's earlier proposals for 09.03.15b that the study already sets aside for Rajaona: the mound may not be a stūpa and a local inscription names the place Ḍakā. Agrees with the study in not choosing Nongarh; adds Asher 2000 as a modern supporter of it.

author: Anand
asr_identification: village Mochārim (24°40′49″ N, 84°59′33″ E), S of the Mahābodhi temple, Gaya district
evidence: Village name (Mochārim/Muchalinda) and an old pond ('Ancient Muchalinda Pond', photograph); 'circumstantial evidence', citing O'Malley, Gaya gazetteer 1906: 46, and his own 2019 post. Uses it as the junction for the shrines to its E (austerities) and S (Kassapa).
quote: circumstantial evidence has fairly established that the village of Mochārim ​​(24° 40' 49'' N. 84° 59' 33'' E) represents the ancient site of the Muchalinda Tank, the place where the Buddha spent his sixth week following the Great Awakening (O'Malley 1906: 46; Anand 2019).
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Agrees with one of the study's open options (Muchharin); adds nothing beyond the name and the pond. Differs from Mizutani (Urel tank).

author: Anand
name_in_asr: stūpa where the Buddha transformed the Kassapa brothers
asr_identification: village Khajawati (24°38′39″ N, 85°00′05″ E), W bank of the Nairañjanā, 1 km S of Kāzichak, Gaya district
evidence: On the ground: Khajawati, like the other villages surveyed, stands on an ancient mound with brick structures under vegetation and a large Brahmanical monastery on top; drone photographs (Vikash Kumar). Placement by sequence from his Kāzichak ('beside' the miracle stūpa); he calls it a 'calculated guess'.
quote: Village Khajawati (24° 38' 39'' N. 85° 00' 05'' E) is situated on the western bank of Nairañjanā, one km further south of Kāzichak, and most likely represents the shrine to mark the transformation of the Kassapa brothers (refer to Map- 2).
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs: the study has only Cunningham's Urel (unlocated in the study). Mizutani gives no site of his own. A guess from relative positions; no find named.

author: Anand
name_in_asr: stūpas where Tapassu and Bhallika offered food and the four Deva-rājas offered bowls
asr_identification: Gothu mound (24°39′12″ N, 85°00′25″ E), E bank of the Nairañjanā, 800 m E of Kāzichak
evidence: On the ground: a 'very prominent' mound of over two acres at Gothu, the village on it; drone photograph; villagers report recent demolition of mounds. The bowl stūpa is put somewhere nearby.
quote: There is a very prominent mound in the village Gothu (24° 39' 12'' N. 85° 00' 25'' E) situated 800 mt precisely east of Kāzichak on the eastern bank of the Nairañjanā river. This prominent mound may very likely represent the site where Tapassu and Bhallika offered food to Buddha (1).
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. New places: 商主奉麨蜜處 and 四天王奉鉢處 stūpas S of the Bodhi tree, not in places.tsv. A guess from position.

author: Anand
name_in_asr: stūpas where the Buddha preached for his mother and showed spiritual changes, by a dry pool
asr_identification: Kāzichak (24°39′11″ N, 84°59′55″ E), W bank of the Nairañjanā, 3 km S of Mochārim, with a large old pond
evidence: On the ground: a large historic pond and an ancient mound under much of the village; drone photographs. The 'dry pool' of the text is the one fixed clue.
quote: The village of Kāzichak (24° 39' 11'' N. 84° 59' 55'' E), located 3km south of Mochārim, boasts a sizable historic pond. Kāzichak is located on the western bank of Nairañjanā. A large part of the village is situated on an ancient mound.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. New places (為母說法處, 現神變處 by the dry pool), not in places.tsv. A guess from the pond.

author: Anand
name_in_asr: stūpas where the Buddha tamed the fire-nāga and where 500 pratyekabuddhas entered nirvāṇa; stūpa where Kassapa came to save the Buddha from the flood
asr_identification: Bhabhani mound (24°39′25″ N, 84°59′18″ E), 2 km NW of Khajawati; Shivrājpur mound (24°39′53″ N, 84°59′44″ E), 1.5 km S of Mochārim, <100 m W of the Nairañjanā
evidence: On the ground: a large mound by the main temple at Bhabhani; at Shivrājpur an ancient mound with an abandoned Brahmanical monastery on it and reused ancient bricks in the shrine. Bearings from the text: NW of the Kassapa stūpa; S of the Mucilinda tank.
quote: the best location for stūpas (6) and (7)—that is, the stūpa to mark the location where the Buddha tamed the Nāga (6) and the stūpa to mark the nirvāṇa place of 500 Pratyeka Buddhas (7)—is the village Bhabhani (24° 39' 25'' N. 84° 59' 18'' E) … an ancient mound in the village Shivrājpur (24° 39' 53'' N. 84° 59' 44'' E) situated 1.5km south of Muchalinda
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. New places (降火龍處, 五百獨覺入涅槃處, 迦葉救如來溺水處), not in places.tsv. Guesses from bearings off his Khajawati and Mochārim.

author: Anand
asr_identification: the excavated mound at the NE corner of Bakrour village, E bank of the Nairañjanā opposite Bodh Gayā
evidence: Reported: ASI Patna Circle excavation 1973 (IAR 1973–74) of the mound locally called Sujātāgaḍh, Sujātākuṭi, Sujātā Quilā: a stūpa in three phases, 2nd c. BCE to 8th–10th c., and 'many seals from 8th-9th CE reading Sujātāgriha' (citing Sinha 2000: 5). On the ground: Bakrour elders and the 95-year-old caretaker of the Bodhgayā maṭha say the mound was always called Sujātāgaḍh; the 19th-c. name Koteni/Katani now names the harvest ground round it. Buchanan (1811) heard from the Mahant that Bakrour was where the Buddha did penance.
quote: A big ancient mound on the north-east corner of Bakrour village was excavated by Patna Circle, Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) in 1973 … Excavation by Shri K N Srivastava led to discovery of many seals from 8th-9th CE reading Sujātāgriha (house of Sujātā) (Sinha 2000: 5). The excavation revealed that stūpa was built in three phases first phase in 2nd BCE and last phase was 8th-10th CE.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Agrees that the Bakraur mound is a major early stūpa (the study's 09.01.01, Gandhahastin stūpa). Adds possible site evidence the study lacks: sealings reading Sujātāgṛha, which would name the monument for Sujātā rather than the Gandhahastin (the study: 'No inscription names the stūpa'; IAR 1973–74 does not mention seals). Check Sinha 2000 and the excavation report before using.

author: Anand
name_in_asr: austerity sites, bathing place in the Nairañjanā, place of Sujātā's offering
asr_identification: E bank of the Nairañjanā around Bakrour: Dharmāraṇya (austerities), Mātaṅgavāpī (food offering), Ratanāgiri rock 200 m E of Bakrour (where the food was eaten, Faxian)
evidence: On the ground: Ratanāgiri rock, c. 12 ft square and 6 ft high, the only rock in the vicinity, found 2018 (Hindustan Times, Patna); Mātaṅgavāpī and Dharmāraṇya on ancient mounds, both Gayā-śrāddha stations, venerated by Buddhist pilgrims only since the 1950s (priests' testimony); 'very prominent' unexcavated mounds NE of Mātaṅgavāpī. Argument: Faxian's distances (3 li W to the bathing place, 2 li N each to the offering place and the rock) and Xuanzang's 'forest E of the Mucilinda tank' and bathing place SW of the austerities fit only the E bank.
quote: These distances and directions mentioned by both Faxian and Xuanzang can be correct only if the events associated with the austerities were on the east bank of river Nairāñjanā as depicted in the map (see figure 2). Dharmāraṇya is the most appropriate location that best meets the description.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs: the study (after Mizutani and Cunningham's plan) has the bathing-place stūpa at Tika Bigha S of Bodh Gayā (low, label only); Anand moves the austerity group across the river E of Bakrour. The rock is Faxian's, not Xuanzang's; the austerity and Sujātā shrines are not separate rows in places.tsv.

author: Anand
name_in_asr: site of Udraka Rāmaputra (pillar), across the river Mahā/Moha
asr_identification: Gāfā Kalān (24°40′55″ N, 85°05′15″ E) or Nāmā/Nawān with the Nāmā Dih mound (24°42′04″ N, 85°04′33″ E), W bank of the Paimār, c. 6 km E of Bakraur, Gaya district; the Mahā = Mohāne
evidence: On the ground: both villages stand on ancient mounds; Nāmā Dih is c. 15 acres, c. 7 ft above the fields, 500 m E of Nāmā on the Paimār, with brickbats; mutilated Buddha and Bodhisattva images in village collectives at both; no trace of the pillar. Argument: the first river E of the Mohāne is the Paimār, and a hermitage should be on a river; Buchanan (1811) saw a pillar at the Koteni (Bakraur) mound, which he takes as Xuanzang's pillar near the four Buddhas' seats.
quote: I have identified two villages Gāfā Kalān (24° 40' 55'' N. 85° 05' 15'' E) and Nāmā/Nawān (24° 42' N. 85° 04' E) that seem to be potential sites for the hermitage of Uddaka mentioned by Xuanzang … I have not found any trace of the pillar mentioned by Xuanzang in Gāfā Kalān or Nāmā.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs: the study leaves 09.01.02 unidentified, to be sought E of the Mohana; Anand gives two candidates there (a 'hunch'). Agrees on the Mahā = Mohana (09.01.02a). The Xiyu ji places the pillar, not the hermitage, beyond the river; the rows are candidates without a pillar.

author: Anand
asr_identification: Gurpā hill, Gaya district (R. D. Banerji 1906); rejects Cunningham's Kurkihar and Stein's Hasra Kol
evidence: On the ground (photographs): remains of a stone stūpa on the summit ascribed to Ajātaśatru; a Mahākassapa image; a votive stūpa; footprints on the summit with a Pāla inscription, worshipped as Viṣṇupāda by Hindu pilgrims in Sāwan. Cited: Patil, Antiquarian Remains in Bihar, pp. 157, 164, 225.
quote: eventually the Gurpa hill (25° 32’ 57 N, 85° 18’ 13 E) identified by R.D. Banerjee in 1906 was accepted as the actual site of Kukkutapādagiri (The Antiquarian remains of Bihar, Dr D.R. Patil, P-157).
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Agrees with the study (Gurpa; not Kurkihar). The Pāla footprint inscription is not read here; worth tracing (it may be the Gurupāda name the study already has from Chhabra's Silao image). The latitude 25°32′57″ is a slip for 24°32′57″ (his 2012 post gives 24°); Hasra Kol's 25°46′ is likewise wrong.

author: Anand
asr_identification: Gurpā hill, Gaya district (Banerji 1906)
evidence: Reported from Banerji, JPASB n.s. 2 (1906): a rectangular 8 × 5 ft tank with one step round its sides, formerly covered by a large stone; when it was opened before 1905 under F. E. Cockshott (railway engineer) a skeleton over 6 ft long was found; many Buddhist sculptures near the tank; the skeleton's fate unknown. Also Chhabra's Silāo image inscription: Kāśyapa 'entered nirvāṇa on the charming hill of Gurupāda' (EI 25: 327). Photographs of the tank, an ancient votive stūpa and a 'footprints of Mahākassapa' sculpture.
quote: Banerji on his visit to Gurpā Hill (Kukkuṭapādagiri) in 1906 noticed a rectangular 8ft X 5ft tank with a single step running along its four sides. Shri Babu Dayal Gupta, guard of the East Indian Railway informed Banerji that this tank was covered with a huge piece of stone.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Agrees with the study (Gurpa). The skeleton story is hearsay reported by Banerji and Anand's reading of it as Mahākassapa's is devotional, not evidence; the tank and sculptures add to the site description.

author: Anand
asr_identification: the cave hill at Ayer (Ayer-Pathri, 24°55′18″ N, 85°14′22″ E), 9 km W of Jeṭhian in the same valley, Gaya/Nalanda border
evidence: On the ground (June 2012): a rock shelter on the steep side of the hill surrounded by brick stūpas of various sizes; fragments of votive stūpas and sandstone Buddha images over the hill, some inscribed; a broken sandstone panel with the ye dharmā creed (read by G. S. Rao, ASI Mysore); structures on the summit; a mound at the foot full of antiquities; Pāla sculpture in the village ('Goraiyan Sthan'). Distances: Ayer c. 40 km N of Gurpa (above 100 li), Jeṭhian 9 km E (30 li). Rejects Cunningham (Buddhain) and Stein (Sahpoor).
quote: Distance and direction of the Buddhavana mentioned by Venerable Xuanzang takes us exactly to the vicinity of Ayer Village(24° 55’ 18 N, 85° 14’ 22 E) … Jeṭhian is exactly 9 km east of the Village Ayer inside the same valley.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs: the study leaves 09.02.01 unidentified (point placed 100 li NE of Gurpa). Anand gives a site with Buddhist remains and the creed, but no inscription naming the place; by his coordinates Ayer is N to slightly NW of Gurpa, not NE as Xuanzang says, while the 30 li E to Jethian fits well. Uses Gurpa (09.01.03) and Jethian (09.02.02) as the study does.

author: Anand
asr_identification: Telhara (Telhada), Nalanda district: the excavated 'Bāladitya mound' at the W end of the village
evidence: On the ground (excavation by the Bihar Directorate of Archaeology from Dec 2009, A. K. Verma): more than 30 trenches on the 'Bāladitya mound'; a Gupta (4th–6th c.) floor across the mound, 5.5 ft of debris, then a Pāla floor; a Gupta wall 6 ft wide with a Pāla wall over it; many sculptures, some inscribed; a late-Pāla (10th c.) inscribed slab warning against harm to the monastery. Earlier: the 40-ft mound at the W end and the mosque at the E end with reused pillars and the 'Teladhaka' inscription (Cunningham, Broadley, Beglar).
quote: A long Gupta period (4th-6th CE) floor running all across the mound has been revealed by different trenches. Over the Gupta floor there is debris of 5.5Ft running all around covered with Pala (8th-12th CE) floor.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Agrees and adds excavated evidence of a Gupta-period establishment, i.e. standing in Xuanzang's time. Primary: Verma, 'Telhara (Nalanda) Excavation – A Brief Report' (Bihar Directorate) and Choudhary et al. 2023. Check whether the 'Bāladitya mound' is the study's Bulandi mound W of the village (same position).

author: Anand
asr_identification: Prāgbodhi = Dungeshwari hill, NE of Bodh Gayā
evidence: None new; states that the identification rests on circumstantial evidence, with no inscription.
quote: Prāgbodhi Hill is yet another Buddhist pilgrimage site, which has been identified on the basis of circumstantial evidence i.e. no inscriptional evidence has been found to support the identification.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Agrees with the study (Mora range, cave on Dhongra = Dungeshwari; medium).

author: Anand
asr_identification: Saraswati, a Hindu shrine on the bank of the Mohāne, c. 2 km NE of Bakrour
evidence: On the ground: a Hindu monastery and shrine (Saraswati) said to stand over an abandoned shrine; a Buddha image recently installed under an old banyan by pilgrims. No find or measurement given.
quote: According to Xuanzang, on the day of Veshākha Pūrṇimā, on his way from Prāgbodhi hill to Bodhi Tree, Bodhisattva Siddhārtha crossed a blind cobra on the bank of River Mohā. The blind cobra regained his eyesight and blessed Bodhisattva Siddhārtha. Later, a shrine was developed there, which got abandoned in the medieval period.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Differs: the study and Mizutani leave the blind nāga's dwelling unidentified. Xuanzang puts it 2–3 li from the E gate of the Bodhi enclosure; Saraswati, beyond Bakrour, is several km away. An assertion, not argued.

author: Anand
asr_identification: the colossal Buddha feet on a lotus pedestal excavated at Nālandā in 1974
evidence: Reported: a 1974 excavation found the feet of a Buddha on a lotus pedestal, large enough for an image of the height Xuanzang gives.
quote: most of these doubts were put to rest when an excavation in 1974 revealed these feet of Buddha on a lotus pedestal. The feet of the statue suggest that the sculpture must have been as tall as Xuanzang described it to be.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Agrees with the study's Sarai mound (Misra, IAR 1975–76) if the feet are those found there; Anand does not name the mound. Xuanzang's image is of copper, the feet presumably brick and stucco.

author: Anand
asr_identification: Marshall's site at the foot of Vaibhāra hill, W of Beglar's cave, Rajgir
evidence: On the ground: at Marshall's site a man-made platform with walled structure beneath, fallen rock from the hill, old foundations and an approach ramp; Beglar's cave has no hall or foundation wall and could not hold 500 monks. Reviews Kittoe/Cunningham/Broadley (Son Bhandar), Beglar (1872) and Marshall.
quote: According to me, the site identified by Marshall for the First Buddhist Council is more convincing than the site proposed by Beglar … One can actually notice the old foundations of the hall and approach ramp at the site identified by Marshall.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Agrees with the study (Marshall's levelled spur on the N face of Vaibhāra, not Son Bhandar).

author: Anand
asr_identification: the cave W of the hot springs cleared by Broadley in 1871, not the small room in the stone platform (Jarāsandha kā baiṭhak) shown to pilgrims
evidence: Cited from Broadley: a chamber 36 × 26 ft, roof 18–20 ft, lined with a 2-ft brick wall, reached by 8–9 brick steps, with a black basalt standing Buddha in the fill. On the ground: the cave now overgrown and in bad shape.
quote: Due to misinformation, in place of this cave, pilgrims currently visit the small room in the large platform (locally called as Jarāsandha kā baithakā) made of dressed stone, as the Pipphaligūhā.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. Broadly agrees with the study (stone house at Jarasandh-ki-baithak with the cave behind it), but treats the cave, not the built 'stone house', as the Pippala; the study follows Marshall in reading 石室 as the platform. Whether Broadley's cave is Cunningham's 40-ft cave behind the platform is not said; Broadley, Buddhistic Remains of Bihar, is the source.

author: Anand
name_in_asr: stūpa of the sermon to Rāhula, left of the road outside the S gate of the New City
asr_identification: an ASI- and Forest-Department-walled plot S of New Rājagṛha, Rajgir (no coordinates)
evidence: On the ground: temporary huts, an ASI boundary wall, no prominent ancient mound.
quote: Xuanzang visited the stūpa, which according to him, was on the left side of the road outside the south gate of the ‘New City’ … The place has no prominent ancient mound.
note: blog, not peer-reviewed. New place: the Rāhula sermon stūpa outside the S gate of New Rājagṛha, not in places.tsv. No evidence that the walled plot is the site; he does not say who first placed it there.

author: Deeg
name_in_asr: great temple built by Bālāditya, N of the Avalokiteśvara temple
asr_identification: no location; the temple is attested at Nālandā by Yaśovarmadeva's inscription
evidence: Inscription: the stone inscription of Yaśovarmadeva's reign found at Nālandā praises a large, shining white prāsāda for the Buddha (Śauddhodani) built by king Bālāditya (Sastri, Nalanda and its Epigraphic Material, p. 79, ll. 8–9; Deeg's translation), and like Xuanzang compares its image with the one on the vajrāsana (l. 19). A Nālandā seal names a Bālāditya-gandhakuṭī (Sastri p. 38), which Deeg links with the pavilion where Xuanzang lodged (Life).
quote: Bālāditya is the only of the Gupta kings named by Xuanzang who develops considerable construction activities outside of the complex monastery and builds a huge temple for an image of Śākyamuni Buddha … by the inscription from the reign of king Yaśovarmadeva found at Nālandā, which highly praises the temple (prāsāda) built for the image of Śākyamuni Buddha (Śauddhodani) by king Bālāditya
note: Adds inscriptional evidence that Bālāditya's temple existed at Nālandā; does not locate it. The study leaves 09.03.x4 unlocated (Cunningham: the high mound at the N end of the stūpa range); the inscription's findspot (Sastri) could bear on which mound.

author: Deeg
asr_identification: Nālandā; Xuanzang's sequence of royal foundations (Śakrāditya, then S, E, N) is an idealised Buddhist lineage, not a building record
evidence: Argument: no archaeological evidence at Nālandā is as early as Xuanzang's date for Śakrāditya ('not long after the nirvāṇa'), and the Gupta names in his list do not follow the inscriptional lineage; Deeg advises keeping the two sets of sources apart. The seal of a Śrī Śakrāditya found at Nālandā 'has nothing to do with' Xuanzang's king (Sastri p. 38).
quote: Such a dating is, of course, impossible because such early archaeological evidence at Nālandā does not exist, but also in the light of the fact that a ruler name Śakrāditya is not known before the Guptas.
note: Agrees with the site (09.03.01); bears on matching Xuanzang's sequence of monasteries to the excavated blocks (09.03.06, 09.03.x2–x4): Deeg reads the sequence as legitimation narrative, so it should not be used as a plan. No new location.

author: Deeg
evidence: Survey of Chinese sources on Bodhgayā (Faxian, Xuanzang, Yijing, Wang Xuance, Song steles of the mid-9th c. to 1033 found in Cunningham's excavations); no site located or tested.
note: No new location; useful only for the Chinese steles (Chavannes 1896) as background to 08.06.04.

author: Deeg
evidence: Lecture abstract: the BHDS–Cardiff 'Xuanzang Trail' project (PIs B. K. Chaudhary and Deeg), four exploration tours 2020–24 in Magadha and N Bihar; names no identifications.
note: Nothing to code until the case studies are published.
